identity.title: Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation)

technique.how: With the patient supine, hook the fingers under the right costal margin at the mid-clavicular line (or press the RUQ) and ask the patient to take a deep breath. A positive sign is abrupt arrest of inspiration as the inflamed gallbladder descends onto the fingers; compare with the same manoeuvre on the left.
technique.prerequisites: Examine before opioid analgesia if feasible, but do not withhold analgesia; patient must be able to follow breathing instructions.

interpretation.positive_finding: Inspiratory arrest with RUQ pain roughly triples the odds of acute cholecystitis (pooled LR+ 2.8) and in an ED cohort was present in 97% of positive hepatobiliary scans.
interpretation.negative_finding: A negative Murphy sign does not exclude cholecystitis; the pooled RCE could not identify any finding with a useful negative LR, so imaging is still needed when suspected.
interpretation.pitfalls: Sensitivity falls in the elderly and after analgesia; other RUQ pathology (hepatitis, perihepatitis) can produce a false positive. Documentation is frequently absent.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: proceed to RUQ ultrasound and treat as probable cholecystitis; negative with ongoing suspicion: still image, do not discharge on exam alone.

estimates.population: Adults with abdominal pain or suspected acute cholecystitis, pooled across included studies (RCE systematic review of 17 studies)
estimates.reference_standard: Surgery, pathology, HIDA scan or RUQ ultrasound, or consistent clinical course
estimates.quote: Possible exceptions were the Murphy sign (positive LR, 2.8; 95% CI, 0.8-8.6) and right upper quadrant tenderness (negative LR, 0.4; 95% CI, 0.2-1.1)

estimates.population: 100 consecutive ED patients referred for urgent HIDA scan, tertiary hospital, retrospective chart review; sign documented in 65
estimates.quote: The presence of Murphy's sign was both sensitive (97.2%) and highly predictive (93.3%) of a positive HBS yet was not documented in 35 cases.

sources.citation: Trowbridge RL, Rutkowski NK, Shojania KG. Does this patient have acute cholecystitis? JAMA. 2003;289(1):80-86.

Singer AJ, McCracken G, Henry MC, Thode HC Jr, Cabahug CJ. Correlation among clinical, laboratory, and hepatobiliary scanning findings in patients with suspected acute cholecystitis. Ann Emerg Med. 1996;28(3):267-272.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a negative sign to exclude cholecystitis in elderly, diabetic or obtunded patients, or after opioid analgesia.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: RUQ pain with fever, jaundice or hypotension suggests cholangitis or gangrenous/perforated cholecystitis: urgent imaging, cultures, antibiotics and surgical/biliary consultation.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: The 2003 RCE found no reliability data for Murphy sign; the Singer cohort noted the sign was undocumented in 35% of charts.

extraction_notes: Pooled LR+ 2.8 (CI crosses 1.0) quoted from the RCE abstract; the RCE text/tables are not reachable, so pooled sensitivity/specificity and LR- are null. Singer 1996 sensitivity 97.2% is against HIDA (not pathology) in a retrospective ED cohort with the sign undocumented in 35/100; specificity is not in the abstract and was not entered. Prevalence 0.53 = 53/100 positive HBS from abstract.
